name: Jump squats

card.summary: A plyometric squat ending in a maximal jump that builds explosive leg power and works the quads, glutes and calves for a more athletic lower body.

quick.overview:
A jump squat is a squat followed by an explosive jump. It trains power in the thighs, hips and calves, the muscles that shape an athletic lower body.

Research describes weighted jump squats improving vertical jump height, and plyometric training more broadly is linked with strength, power and bone density gains.
quick.how: People perform them bodyweight or with a light load as part of lower-body or conditioning sessions, landing softly. Because they are demanding, they are generally programmed as a short, high-quality block rather than for fatigue.
quick.risks: Plyometrics produce large forces on joints and tendons, so reference sources advise good baseline strength and technique before starting.

lead: Jump squats combine a squat with a maximal vertical jump and are a standard plyometric exercise for building explosive power.[1] They train the quads, glutes and calves, and are done bodyweight or with a light load.

For appearance, they are used as part of lower-body and conditioning work aimed at a more athletic, muscular lower body: explosive efforts recruit fast-twitch muscle, and jump training is a common component of programmes that report performance gains alongside muscle growth.[6] Research reviews find that weighted jump squats increase vertical jump height, and that power output depends on load.[2][3] Fatigue after a jump-squat session was reported to resolve within about 48 hours in one trial.[4]

chain: Builds power and trains fast-twitch muscle
angle.text: Jump squats train the lower body for power. Heavier jump training is also used in programmes that report hypertrophy alongside performance gains.

paras: The movement is a squat followed by a jump as high as possible; it is among the common plyometric exercises.[1] Wikipedia lists squat jumps alongside tuck jumps, box jumps, depth jumps and broad jumps as standard lower-body plyometrics.[1] Variants include bodyweight jump squats, jump squats with a light barbell or other external load, and loaded versions performed on a machine.[3]

Plyometrics use the stretch-shortening cycle, in which a muscle switches quickly from lengthening to shortening. Landing forces are absorbed by eccentric contraction, and the brief turnaround phase between landing and take-off lets elastic energy stored mostly in the tendons contribute to the jump.[1] Wikipedia describes the sequence of take-off as moving from hip to knee to ankle.[1]

Wikipedia reports that Soviet Olympians adopted plyometric-style jumping in the 1950s, that Yuri Verkhoshansky developed the original depth-jump-based "shock method" in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and that former US distance runner Fred Wilt coined the term "plyometrics" after watching Soviet athletes jump in warm-ups, promoting it with Michael Yessis in the early 1980s.[1] The US-popularised version includes any jump regardless of ground contact time, which is the context in which jump squats are used.[1]

People include jump squats in leg days, athletic training and conditioning circuits to build power and a more athletic lower body.[1] In an 8-week trial of young ice hockey players, a lower-body programme of heavy squats and explosive jump squats improved strength, power and muscle thickness, though the programme compared two loading methods rather than testing jump squats alone.[6] Wikipedia also notes that a one-year trial of high-intensity jump training in men with low bone density increased lumbar spine and whole-body bone mineral density, and that plyometrics combined with other neuromuscular training can reduce lower-limb injuries in team sports.[1]

A review found weighted jump squats raise vertical jump height but were no more effective than plyometric depth jumps.[2] Another review on transfer to sprinting concluded that bilateral vertical movements such as jump squats transfer minimally to sprint acceleration, while unilateral and horizontal plyometrics showed larger gains, and noted that general strength work can help body mass and injury risk.[5] A review of methods for determining the load that maximises jump-squat power found that differing data-collection protocols produce contradictory results and proposed a standardised protocol.[3]

Plyometrics produce large forces on joints and tendons, so reference sources describe them as suited to well-conditioned people with good technique.[1] Wikipedia cites guidance that participants build baseline strength, flexibility and proprioception first, land with a slight knee and hip bend, avoid overtraining, and be supervised if prepubescent or older.[1]

In an RCT of ten male athletes, jump squats (10 x 5) produced fatigue that resolved by 48 hours, compared with 72 hours for heavy back squats and sprinting.[4] An 8-week randomized trial in 22 young ice hockey players used heavy squats and explosive jump squats within a programme that improved performance and, in one group, muscle hypertrophy.[6] A review addressed methods for determining optimal jump-squat load.[3] Reviews of resisted jump and sprint training found weighted jump squats increased vertical jump height.[2] Randomised trials in rugby and basketball players have also used jump squats as part of loaded, potentiation and vertical-oriented training protocols.[7][8][9]
